evaluation.name: Project Description, Project Structure and Security Policy

children.name: Project Description
children.reason:
Evaluation of the README file:

project_purpose:
Score (avg): 5.0
[QWEN] The README clearly and thoroughly describes both what the project is and why it is useful. The opening paragraph states: "CIB seven is a flexible framework for workflow and process automation. Its core is a native BPMN 2.0 process engine that runs inside the Java Virtual Machine," and explains its value proposition ("It can be embedded inside any Java application and any Runtime Container. It integrates with Java EE 6 and is a perfect match for the Spring Framework."). The "Components" section itemizes the concrete capabilities (Engine, REST API, Spring/CDI Integration, Camunda Modeler, Cockpit, Admin, Tasklist) organized by BPM lifecycle stage (Implementation/Execution, Design, Operations, Human Task Management), and the "A Framework" section further justifies the value with "Highly Integrable" and "Embeddable" subsections, including the statement "We seek to deliver a great experience to developers that want to use BPM technology in their projects." A reader can fully understand the project's purpose and utility from this README alone.

setup_instructions:
Score (avg): 3.0
[QWEN] The README does not contain any actual setup or build instructions inline. There are no prerequisites (e.g., required JDK version), no build commands (Maven/Gradle), no installation steps, and no quick-start code snippets. The only setup-related content is a pointer to external documentation: the "Getting Started: https://docs.cibseven.org/get-started/" link in the top link list, a "manual-latest" badge linking to the external manual, and a "Tests" section that merely says "To run the tests in this repository, please see our testing tips and tricks (TESTING.md)." While delegating documentation to an external site and separate repo files is a common and reasonable practice for a large platform, the README itself describes none of the setup steps, so it only partially satisfies this criterion.

info_project_status:
Score (avg): 1.0
[QWEN] The README contains no explicit statement about the project's status. There is no version number or release badge (only a "manual-latest" documentation badge and a "discussions" badge), no statement such as "actively developed," "stable," "in development," or "no longer maintained," and no description of the current release cycle or maintenance policy. While the presence of links to an Issue Tracker (https://github.com/cibseven/cibseven/issues) and a Discussions forum implicitly suggests the project is alive, these are contact channels, not a description of project status. A reader cannot determine from this README whether the project is actively developed, in maintenance mode, or abandoned.

info_maintainer:
Score (avg): 2.0
[QWEN] The README only partially addresses this criterion. It includes a "Contributing" section: "Please see our contribution guidelines (CONTRIBUTING.md) for how to raise issues and how to contribute code to our project," which describes how to contribute but not who the maintainers are. It also mentions "Community Extensions ... provided and maintained by our great open source community," which hints at a community-driven model. However, the README never explicitly states who maintains the core project (e.g., no organization name, no maintainer list, no contact email or dedicated team reference), so a reader cannot learn from the README alone who is responsible for maintaining CIB seven.

children.name: Project Structure
children.reason:
Project structure evaluation:

directory_organization:
Score (avg): 4.0
[QWEN] As a large Java/Maven monorepo, the project follows the standard Maven multi-module layout almost universally: every Java module uses src/main/java, src/main/resources, src/test/java, src/test/resources (e.g., engine/src, commons/logging/src, connect/http-client/src, model-api/bpmn-model/src) with a pom.xml at each module root, an aggregator/parent at parent/pom.xml, and the Maven wrapper (mvnw, mvnw.cmd). The Node/JS side follows its own conventions (webapps/frontend/package.json, webpack.common.js, webpack.dev.js, webpack.prod.js, .eslintrc, .prettierrc), CI follows GitHub/Jenkins conventions (.github/workflows/*.yml, .ci/daily/Jenkinsfile, .ci/main-trigger/Jenkinsfile), IDE tooling is grouped in settings/ (eclipse, intellij-idea, maven), and documentation sits at the root (README.md, CONTRIBUTING.md, TESTING.md, SECURITY.md) and in docs/ folders (engine-rest/docs, qa/performance-tests-engine/docs). This is strongly conventional, so it earns at least a 4. It falls short of a 5 due to a few irregularities: javaee/jobexecutor-ra places META-INF/MANIFEST.MF at the module root instead of under src/main/resources; distro/wildfly/distro/src contains an EMPTY_FILE placeholder; versioned duplicate trees exist (distro/run vs distro/run4, qa/tomcat-runtime vs qa/tomcat10-runtime, plus resources-tomcat10/resources-tomcat11 in qa/integration-tests-engine); and the stub spring-boot-4-starter module has an awkward nesting (starter-client/spring-boot/pom.xml with only poms and no sources).

naming_conventions:
Score (avg): 4.0
[QWEN] The dominant convention is consistent kebab-case for modules and files: engine-rest, engine-dmn, engine-cdi, model-api, spring-boot-starter, quarkus-extension, test-utils, internal-dependencies, freemarker-template-engine, and files such as .github/workflows/add-issue-to-project.yml, java-dependency-check.yml, sync-label-colors.yml, .ci/scripts/alignment/check-spring-alignment.sh and alignment-lib.sh, settings/maven/nexus-settings.xml and docker-compose.yml. Tool-mandated names are used correctly everywhere (pom.xml, Jenkinsfile, assembly.xml, .gitignore). However, consistency is visibly undermined by an incomplete rebrand from Camunda to "cibseven": bom/camunda-bom and bom/camunda-only-bom exist in a project named cib-seven; webapps/frontend contains camunda-bpm-sdk-js and camunda-commons-ui; test resources are named camunda.cfg.xml (and even activiti.cfg.xml in engine-cdi/core), while other artifacts use the new name (cibseven-webclient.properties, start-cibseven.sh/shutdown-cibseven.bat, distro/cibseven-welcome); and engine/src/test/java contains both org/camunda and org/cibseven packages. Other stray inconsistencies include renovate_camunda.json5 (snake_case next to its kebab sibling renovate.json5), publiccode_logo.svg (snake_case) vs publiccode.yml, BpmPlatform.xsd (PascalCase) in engine vs bpm-platform.xml (kebab-case) in qa runtimes, the all-caps placeholder EMPTY_FILE, camunda.cfg.prefix_extended.xml (snake suffix), two start/stop script styles (plain run.sh/start.bat vs start-cibseven.sh), and mixed doc formats (README.md, README.adoc, README.asciidoc, README.txt). These are real but mostly cosmetic, so 4 is fair.

separation_of_concerns:
Score (avg): 5.0
[QWEN] Concerns are separated clearly and deliberately. Production code (src/main) is separated from unit tests (src/test) in virtually every module. Quality-assurance work is isolated in a top-level qa/ tree — integration-tests-engine, integration-tests-webapps, large-data-tests, performance-tests-engine, test-db-indexes-in-scripts, test-db-instance-migration, test-db-rolling-update — so heavy integration/perf/DB tests do not pollute module unit tests. Reusable test infrastructure is isolated in test-utils/ (archunit, assert, junit5-extension, junit5-extension-dmn, testcontainers). Build and dependency configuration is separated into parent/, bom/, and internal-dependencies/, while IDE tooling lives in settings/ (eclipse, intellij-idea, maven). CI is kept out of the source in .ci/ (config/matrices.yaml, stage-types.yaml, per-pipeline Jenkinsfiles, alignment scripts) and .github/ (workflows, ISSUE_TEMPLATE, renovate configs). Documentation is separated at the root (README.md, CONTRIBUTING.md, TESTING.md, SECURITY.md, LICENSE, NOTICE, publiccode.yml) and via per-module READMEs. Artifacts are also cleanly divided: engine (core runtime), engine-rest (with its docs/ OpenAPI build), webapps (Java assembly module vs frontend/ JS code), distro (server targets, welcome static assets, license-book, sql-script), and examples/ for samples. Only minor mixing remains — webapps bundles a Java assembly module and the JS frontend together, and distro aggregates several distribution sub-concerns — but subdirectories keep them apart, so the overall separation is excellent.

modularity:
Score (avg): 5.0
[QWEN] The breakdown of the codebase into modules is logical and unusually deep. Functional boundaries are respected: core runtime (engine), DMN with its FEEL implementations as separate modules (engine-dmn/engine, feel-api, feel-juel, feel-scala, bom), REST API split into engine-rest, engine-rest-openapi (schema.json + FTL templates) and engine-rest-openapi-generator; framework integrations as independent modules (engine-cdi/core, engine-spring/core and core-7, quarkus-extension following the standard deployment/runtime split, spring-boot-starter split by concern into starter, starter-client, starter-rest, starter-security, starter-test, starter-webapp, starter-webapp-core); model APIs separated (model-api/bpmn-model, cmmn-model, dmn-model, xml-model); shared libraries (commons/logging, typed-values, utils, testing; juel; freemarker-template-engine); a plugin architecture (engine-plugins/connect-plugin, identity-ldap, identity-scim, spin-plugin; connect/core, http-client, soap-http-client, ai-agent, connectors-all, with its own bom); data-format plugins (spin/core, dataformat-json-jackson, dataformat-xml-dom, dataformat-all); Java EE artifacts (javaee/ejb-client, ejb-service, jobexecutor-ra, jobexecutor-rar); a Java client (clients/java); and per-target distributions (distro/tomcat, wildfly, jboss, run, run4, webjar, sql-script, license-book, cibseven-welcome). BOMs (bom/, connect/bom/, spin/bom/, engine-dmn/bom/, commons/bom/) plus internal-dependencies/ and parent/pom.xml indicate a well-managed dependency graph. Minor blemishes exist — version-duplicated modules (distro/run vs run4, qa/tomcat-runtime vs tomcat10-runtime/tomcat11, test-fixture-11 through test-fixture-30), the in-progress spring-boot-4-starter mirroring spring-boot-starter, and vendored frontend libraries inside webapps/frontend — but the overall modularity is excellent for a project of this scale.

children.name: Security Policy
children.reason:
Evaluation of the SECURITY.md file:

security_contact_information:
Score (avg): 3.0
[QWEN] The document provides a clear link for security-related reporting: “here through github” with the URL https://github.com/cibseven/cibseven/security/advisories/new. This gives users a direct way to submit security concerns via GitHub. However, it does not provide additional contact details such as a security email address, responsible team, PGP key, or alternative contact method, so it is acceptable but not fully comprehensive for all security-related inquiries.

vulnerability_reporting_process:
Score (avg): 4.0
[QWEN] The document clearly states that vulnerabilities should be reported through GitHub and provides the exact destination: “report it here through github” with the link to create a new security advisory. This makes the reporting process straightforward for users. It does not provide further details, such as what information to include, expected response time, or handling steps, but the basic process of where to report is clear.

supported_versions:
Score (avg): 1.0
[QWEN] The document does not specify which versions of the software are currently supported with security updates. There is no mention of supported release versions, end-of-life policies, version support windows, or which releases will receive security patches. Therefore, this criterion is not met.
